name: Neil Melanson Kimura System
description: Study Neil Melanson kimura variations with a focused course companion linking double-wrist control, guard and half-guard decisions to practical learning tasks.
summary: The Neil Melanson Kimura System is a BJJGraph study guide for using double-wrist control across positional changes and comparing related shoulder-lock configurations.
overview:
The Filthy Kimura offers Neil Melanson's specific approach to double-wrist control, including power and Ground Marshal variations, defensive problems, and sequences from guard and half guard. It adds a distinct instructor perspective to the existing kimura material on BJJGraph.

This page supplies an original study plan rather than reproducing the course. The main question is whether a useful connection survives as the position changes. A kimura grip can help organise movement, but holding the hands together does not automatically mean the shoulder is controlled. Compare a small number of configurations and keep all joint-lock pressure out of the transition drill until a coach has checked the position.
key_principles: Distinguish keeping the double-wrist grip from controlling the shoulder.
Study a positional change before adding its finishing pressure.
Compare named kimura variations by their contact and alignment.
Notice whether a defensive frame blocks entry or merely changes the available branch.
Retain a guard or top-position fallback when the grip no longer provides control.
Use deliberate movement and immediate release around shoulder locks.

key_components.description: Inspect the two-on-one arm connection and identify when the defender can still move their shoulder despite the grip.
key_components.purpose: Build a clear standard for useful control.

key_components.description: Compare a familiar kimura with one demonstrated Melanson variation while keeping the starting position the same.
key_components.purpose: Identify the different problem the variation addresses.

key_components.description: Have the defender place an agreed frame and distinguish difficulty reaching the grip from difficulty moving after it is established.
key_components.purpose: Choose a relevant study topic instead of increasing force.

key_components.description: Track the targeted arm as a cooperative partner changes between agreed guard and half-guard contexts.
key_components.purpose: Test whether the connection remains functional during movement.

implementation_sequence.description: Begin with a basic kimura configuration both partners know. Stop before shoulder pressure and identify the controlled arm.
Let the defender make a small, agreed movement. Observe whether the grip carries useful control or merely follows the wrist.
Study a selected Melanson configuration with a coach and repeat the same movement test from the same starting point.
Ask the defender to supply one frame. Separate the work needed to enter the grip from the work needed to move afterward.
Rehearse an agreed guard-to-half-guard change while retaining or deliberately releasing the kimura connection. End at a stable position.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The hands stay connected while the shoulder becomes free.
common_obstacles.solution: Use the shoulder-freedom test and review the surrounding body position.
Compare two configurations side by side and record the problem each is intended to solve.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The attacker tries to move through a firm frame by twisting the arm.
common_obstacles.solution: Reset and identify whether the frame is an entry obstacle or a positional obstacle.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Losing the kimura grip also loses guard.
common_obstacles.solution: Rehearse deliberate release to a familiar guard before increasing resistance.

assessment_metrics.description: Assess whether the connection actually limits shoulder movement.
Explain one difference between two studied configurations.
Classify the defender's frame by the phase it interrupts.
Observe the arm connection during a guard change.
proficiency_indicators: Recovers guard when control is lost

training_methodology.drilling_approach: BJJGraph suggests a grip-without-finish exercise. From half guard, establish an agreed double-wrist connection and let the partner move their shoulder slightly. Compare the result with one coach-approved variation, then add a single frame. The objective is to explain the connection, not to move the shoulder farther or win a grip contest.

progression_path.focus: Recognise basic double-wrist control without finishing pressure.
Test one alternative configuration against the same movement.
Identify what an agreed defensive frame changes.
Carry or deliberately release the connection during a guard transition.

common_mistakes: Assuming a locked grip always means a controlled shoulder.
Changing several kimura variations before understanding the first.
Using shoulder rotation to force a positional transition.

flashcards.question: Why is a kimura grip not proof of shoulder control?
flashcards.answer: The hands can remain connected while the defender still moves their shoulder freely; assess the surrounding position as well as the grip.

flashcards.question: How should two kimura variations be compared?
flashcards.answer: Use the same starting context and defensive movement so the difference in contact or control can be identified clearly.

flashcards.question: What distinction helps diagnose a defensive frame?
flashcards.answer: Determine whether the frame prevents obtaining the grip or prevents positional movement after the grip has already been established.

flashcards.question: What is a useful goal for a kimura movement drill?
flashcards.answer: Reach a stable position while tracking the targeted shoulder, or deliberately release to guard when the connection stops being useful.

flashcards.question: How should shoulder-lock pressure be handled during transition practice?
flashcards.answer: Keep it out of the control drill, move deliberately and release immediately on a tap or any request to stop.

flashcards.question: Why practise releasing the kimura to guard?
flashcards.answer: A reliable release gives a positional fallback when the grip no longer controls the shoulder and discourages forcing a lost attack.

products.title: The Filthy Kimura
products.blurb: A distinct kimura perspective covering double-wrist variants, frame problems and guard-to-half-guard sequences.
products.best_for: Students familiar with basic kimura control who want another instructor's approach; several catch-influenced arm locks need selective coached practice.
products.study_focus: Compare the foundational double-wrist material with the movement drill and half-guard sequence before adding more variations.
products.practice_tip: BJJGraph suggestion: test whether the shoulder remains controlled while the hands stay connected, using no finishing pressure.
